tldr: Without any prior mapping traversals, this work builds a topological graph directly from a floor plan and human-provided photos or notes. Combining node-by-node visual verification with human–robot memory co-updating, it achieves accurate and rapid indoor navigation.
hero_caption: Comparison of the setup workflows between conventional methods and AVALON. Conventional methods require the robot to pre-traverse the site to build a global map, taking twice as long. AVALON only needs a floor plan and photos from a human, significantly shortening the time to first arrival without prior runs.
overview:
When deploying service robots to a new environment, humans already know the building's layout and traffic rules. Yet robots typically require long pre-mapping traversals (collecting data for SLAM). Needing site-specific training or pre-traversals causes significant time loss when immediate robot deployment is desired.

To address this, the authors propose AVALON, a framework that transfers human prior spatial knowledge to the robot as topological memory to execute tasks immediately without pre-mapping. It automatically extracts a walkable topological skeleton from a floor plan, associating human-taken daily photos, language landmarks, and traffic rules node by node. The robot does not maintain a high-precision global SLAM map. Instead, it navigates between nodes using a local policy, verifies arrival at target nodes using a vision-language model (VLM), and resets translational drift in odometry. Furthermore, it introduces a mechanism where the robot actively verifies human-reported environmental changes in-situ based on task relevance to co-update shared memory.

In real-world experiments using a quadruped robot (Unitree Go2) in an office environment, AVALON reduced total mission time by 40.9% compared to a conventional pre-mapping baseline (DimOS). In addition, long-range traversals that failed with policy-only execution succeeded in all trials thanks to translational re-anchoring at nodes, also demonstrating adaptability to environmental changes.
contributions: Designed a topological spatial memory deployable solely from floor plans and human-provided clues, completely eliminating on-site pre-traversal and site-specific training.
Proposed a translational re-anchoring mechanism that combines a local goal-following policy with VLM-based node arrival verification, resetting cumulative drift without global SLAM.

Constructed a human–robot memory co-updating framework that separates human permissions (e.g., access rules) from robot physical observations (e.g., blocked paths) and performs in-situ validation gated by task relevance.
Demonstrated superiority over pre-mapping approaches and map-free policies as well as adaptability to environmental changes using a physical quadruped robot.

sections.heading: Leveraging Human Knowledge Directly for Navigation in a Robot's Unseen Environment
sections.summary: Even if a building is familiar to humans, it is completely unseen to a robot. AVALON builds a topological skeleton from human-provided floor plans and photos, enabling immediate execution of the first navigation mission without prior mapping.
sections.details:
When deploying service robots in real-world environments, humans already know the layout and restricted areas. Even so, conventional autonomous navigation systems require the robot to roam the site and construct a SLAM map, creating a major deployment bottleneck.

Here is the key insight: if humans could simply hand the robot a floor plan drawing, room photos taken on a smartphone, and simple notes, the preliminary traversal exploration could be skipped entirely. AVALON (Asymmetric Visual-Architectural Layered Online Navigation) realizes this idea through three core pillars: seeding, execution, and co-updating.

First, it generates a skeleton (nodes and edges) allowing straight-line traversals from a floor plan, binding human-provided clues with shared IDs. The robot follows this skeleton using a local obstacle-avoidance policy. When arriving at a target node, it strictly verifies "is this really the place?" using vision-language models (VLMs). Translational drift is corrected (re-anchored) at successfully verified nodes, allowing the robot to reach its goal despite odometry drift without needing an accurate global map.

Furthermore, the division of labor between human and robot is smart. Humans report unobservable constraints like "room closed for meeting" or environmental changes like "a cart was placed in the hallway." The robot physically verifies this on-site and updates the memory only when that information is relevant to its current task. This asymmetric fusion of human and robot strengths is a major feature of this method.

sections.heading: Crucial Differences from CAD Priors, Exploratory SLAM, and Map-Free Policies
sections.summary: Prior approaches range widely from CAD utilization and topological exploration to map-free reinforcement learning policies. AVALON uniquely ties human knowledge to in-situ observations under the same graph IDs without any preliminary robot traversal.
sections.details:
Let's break down the differences between related work and AVALON across several categories.

### II-A Floor Plans and CAD Priors
Using architectural drawings or CAD data for robots (such as osmAG-Nav) has been explored before. However, most conventional studies assume high-precision LiDAR alignment, often requiring pre-existing point clouds or maps of the site. AVALON compiles the floor plan into a visibility-constrained point-goal skeleton, attaching photos and text to stable node IDs to manage progress through visual semantics without LiDAR maps or pre-traversals.

### II-B Two-Stage Mapping and Autonomous Exploration
Metric SLAM like RTAB-Map and topological navigation methods like NTS and TSGM require the robot to explore the site beforehand, build a map, and then navigate. In other words, a data-collection pre-traversal phase was mandatory. AVALON initializes a skeleton with pre-existing nodes and edges directly from a floor plan, enabling immediate travel toward the destination on the very first run.

### II-C Map-Free Policies and Zero-Shot Exploration
Recent advances in reinforcement learning for local goal-following (such as NavDP and X-NavDP) allow robots to reach goals while avoiding obstacles without a map. However, these struggle and get stuck over long, occluded paths or complex layouts. AVALON uses these policies as local executors while relying on the higher-level topological skeleton and node verification to reliably complete long-range navigation.

### II-D Human–Robot Memory Co-Updating
Human-in-the-loop SLAM systems exist where humans adjust map labels, but AVALON's co-updating operates at the task level. It uniquely employs an asymmetric separation of authority: humans define permissions, while the robot verifies physical reality.

sections.heading: System Design: From Skeleton Generation to Node Verification and Co-Updating
sections.summary: A visibility-constrained skeleton graph is extracted from a floor plan and coupled with human multimodal clues. The robot moves between nodes via a local policy, resets translational drift upon VLM- and odometry-gated arrival checks, and co-updates memory with humans.
sections.details:
The AVALON system consists of three components: layered spatial memory construction, node-verified topological execution, and evidence-gated memory co-updating.

### III-A System Overview and Problem Formulation
The system maintains a graph $G=(V, E)$ generated from a floor plan. Each node has a unique, stable ID associated with photos and text notes. Odometry and topological coordinate frames undergo a one-time initial alignment at startup, without building a global SLAM map or performing prior runs.

### III-B Human-Seeded Layered Spatial Memory
First, walkable space $\mathcal{F}$ is extracted from a raster floor plan image via wall thresholding and exterior flood-filling. Thinning extracts nodes (endpoints and junctions), and an edge is created only when a straight orthogonal segment between two nodes lies entirely within the walkable space (checked using Bresenham's algorithm). Waypoints are inserted at occluded corners to guarantee straight local hops.

Here, the division of node roles is interesting. Nodes are divided into Semantic Nodes and simple Connector Waypoints. Junctions with high visual openness (VGA openness score) are set as semantic nodes, where humans attach photos and text descriptions. In contrast, connector waypoints at turns are used solely for movement, skipping image verification stops. This minimizes unnecessary verification overhead and ensures smooth traversal.

### III-C Node Verification and Translational Re-Anchoring
During transit, the robot follows nodes sequentially using a local policy (NavDP or X-NavDP). Upon entering a semantic node's verification zone, the robot stops and compares multi-view camera images with stored images and text via a VLM (Qwen3.5-Omni).

Verification also utilizes an odometry distance-range gate. Node arrival is declared only when the actual integrated distance $d_k^{\mathrm{odom}}$ from the previous confirmed node falls within the range $[\alpha \ell_k, \beta \ell_k]$ around the nominal path length $\ell_k(v)$. Once arrival is verified, translational offset $t_{k+1}$ is updated using the node's map coordinates and current odometry as shown in Eq. (4) (keeping orientation $R_0$ fixed). Thus, cumulative translational drift is cleanly interrupted at each node without requiring orientation correction or a SLAM map.

### III-D Evidence-Gated Human–Robot Memory Co-Updating
Each memory element $x$ separately tracks robot-observed physical state $s_t(x) \in \{\text{unknown, clear, blocked}\}$, language description $\ell_t(x)$, and human-assigned permission $p_t(x) \in \{\text{allowed, forbidden}\}$. When a human reports that a passage is blocked, it is held only as a hypothesis. The robot physically verifies it using cameras and depth sensors only when its current navigation task requires passing through that route. The physical state is updated only after verification, preventing confusion caused by inaccurate reports.

sections.heading: Validation on the Go2 Quadruped: Cutting Deployment Time by 40% Without Mapping
sections.summary: Experiments on a physical Unitree Go2 compared AVALON against a pre-mapping baseline (DimOS) and standalone map-free policies. AVALON eliminated pre-traversal, reduced deployment time by 40.9%, and proved robust against odometry noise.
sections.details:
To evaluate the proposed method, real-world experiments were conducted in an office environment using a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot.

### IV-A Experimental Setup
The robot was equipped with an omnidirectional camera (Insta360 X3), an RGB-D camera (Intel RealSense D455F), and a Jetson AGX Orin. The local policy (NavDP / X-NavDP) ran on an external workstation (RTX 5090) communicating via ROS 2 to produce local waypoints at 6 Hz. Semantic node arrival was verified via API calls to Qwen3.5-Omni, while YOLO-World was used for in-situ object detection. Two evaluation routes were tested: Intersection-to-Dining (12.81 m) and Dining-to-Conference (20.43 m).

Baselines included DimOS-Go2, which maps the entire area with LiDAR and odometry before autonomous navigation, and policy-only baselines (NavDP / X-NavDP) given only global goals without AVALON's topological graph or node verification.

### IV-B Inter-Room Navigation Performance
On the Intersection-to-Dining route, AVALON with X-NavDP completed the mission with a total robot operating time of 46.4 s (5/5 success) from deployment to finish without pre-mapping. In contrast, DimOS-Go2 required 45.2 s for mapping and 33.3 s for navigation, totaling 78.5 s (4/5 success). AVALON reduced total robot time by 40.9%. While pure transit time during navigation was slightly slower for AVALON due to pauses for node verification, skipping pre-mapping traversals far outweighed that difference.

Meanwhile, standalone X-NavDP without a graph wandered near the start on long occluded paths, timing out at 120 s in all 5 runs.

### IV-C Robustness to Odometry Noise and Co-Updating Case Study
Experiments with intentional Gaussian noise and random-walk drift added to odometry (noise scales 0.02 and 0.04) were also conducted. While navigation time slightly increased under higher noise, the robot reached the goal in all trials. Because translational drift is corrected at every semantic node, cumulative errors do not diverge.

Additionally, on the Dining-to-Conference route, the robot tested an in-situ validation scenario where a human reported "a cart at the office entrance." The robot navigated to that node, confirmed the entrance was unblocked, updated memory to "clear," and successfully reached the conference room across all 5 runs.

sections.heading: Summary and Outlook: A Topology-First Paradigm for Autonomous Navigation
sections.summary: Instead of relying on rigid global SLAM maps, AVALON realizes immediately deployable zero-shot autonomous navigation through human-seeded topological memory, node verification, and asymmetric memory co-updating.
sections.details:
This paper presented AVALON, a framework that enables robots to navigate using human floor plans and prior knowledge rather than building global geometric maps from scratch.

In summary, the robot follows a floor-plan-derived topological skeleton using a local policy and resets translational error at key semantic nodes verified by a VLM. By properly decoupling human permissions from robot physical observations and updating memory based on task relevance, highly reliable navigation is achieved without on-site pre-traversal.

Physical quadruped experiments demonstrated a 40.9% reduction in deployment time compared to a pre-mapping baseline, achieving a 100% success rate on long-range navigation where map-free policies failed completely. This offers a highly practical and sound approach toward a world where robots can be brought to a new site and operate immediately.

takeaways: Challenged the assumption that high-precision global SLAM maps are mandatory, proving that a floor plan skeleton combined with key visual verification (translational reset) suffices for indoor navigation.
High practical utility of converting everyday human information (floor plans, smartphone photos, notes) directly into executable robot memory structures.
Asymmetric co-updating design that avoids blindly accepting human reports (hypotheses), updating memory only after robot in-situ validation triggered by task relevance.
limitations: Re-anchoring at node arrival only corrects translational (positional) drift, leaving odometry yaw (rotation) drift and floor plan geometric distortions uncorrected.
Pausing at every semantic node for VLM verification causes frequent transit interruptions, resulting in slower pure travel times.
Online estimation of local policy error tolerance ($\Delta_{\pi, c}$) and enforcement of theoretical connectivity guarantees during skeleton generation are not yet implemented.
